post.title: Compound AI Systems Are Plumbing, Not Intelligence
post.content:
Every few months a new framework promises to make your LLM "actually useful." The roadmap usually looks the same: retrieval, tool calling, memory, a second agent that reviews the first one's output. The system gets more impressive in demos. The model inside stays the same.

I have been running experiments on this for most of this year. Not formal benchmarks — just watching where outputs actually change when you modify the system architecture versus when you swap the underlying model. The pattern that keeps showing up: infrastructure changes improve reliability curves. Model changes improve capability ceilings. These are different things.

What compound AI systems are good at:
- Reducing variance in outputs (same input → more consistent output)
- Covering edge cases that would otherwise require prompt engineering
- Making late-stage errors (wrong tool, wrong document) less frequent
- Giving you observability into where failures happen

What they are not good at:
- Giving a model new reasoning capabilities it did not have
- Substituting for a model that cannot follow multi-step chains of thought
- Compensating for a weak base model with strong scaffolding

The clearest signal I found: take any pipeline that uses retrieval + generation + verification + memory. Now replace the underlying model with a significantly weaker one. The pipeline degrades in ways that no amount of orchestration fixes. Now do the reverse — keep the same model, strip away all the pipeline machinery, and give it a well-crafted prompt. The capability drop is smaller than you would expect.

This is not an argument against compound systems. It is an argument against the conflation. When you read that "agentic RAG" or "multi-agent orchestration" dramatically improves performance, what you are usually seeing is the pipeline handling cases the base model was already bad at, but doing nothing for cases where the model's reasoning was the bottleneck.

The framing matters because it changes where you spend your engineering budget. If compound AI is intelligence, you should keep adding components. If it is plumbing, you should ask whether your model is the actual constraint — and if it is, no amount of memory or tool use will substitute for a stronger base.

What I do not have full data on: whether certain architectures — feedback loops, self-revision, tree-of-thought — are genuinely different, where the pipeline itself enables reasoning the base model could not do. My honest read is that some of these are real, but they are rarer than the marketing suggests, and they are harder to build reliably than the demos imply.

Compound AI systems are the best way to get consistent, observable behavior from an unreliable reasoning engine. They are not a path to reasoning that exceeds the underlying model's capacity.

That framing has been more useful to me than any benchmark.

---

Here's a test: can you identify which of your pipeline improvements changed the reliability curve versus which ones changed the capability ceiling? Those are different bets — and mixing them up is where engineering budgets go wrong.
